newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka plantation IPOs likely to be snapped up.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka plantation IPOs likely to be snapped up.

text.p: Initial public offers (IPO) of Sri Lankan estate firms are expected to sell out quickly when they hit the market from September, analysts said on Monday.
Judging by the impressive growth of shares in plantation firms already listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE), the issues may well be oversubscribed.
"With tea and even rubber prices expected to be good in the future too, the IPOs should be snapped up," said Rajive Casie Chitty of brokerage CT Smith.

The Public Enterprise Reform Commission (PERC) said on Monday it would begin rolling out from September IPOs of seven estate firms, in which 51 percent stakes were sold to strategic investors in 1996.

Twenty percent, or four million 10-rupee (17-cent) shares, would be sold of the issued capital of Watawala Plantations, Maskeliya Plantations, Madulsima Plantations, Hapugastenne Plantations and Balangoda Plantations.
Twenty percent of Agarapatana Plantations and Udapussellawa Plantations would also be sold, but in their case this would comprise 2.9 million and 1.9 million shares respectively.
"We expect to roll them one-by-one, every two weeks starting from about the beginning of September," an official of PERC, the state arm which oversees privatisations, told Reuters.
Market analysts said the public response should be favourable with every broker recommending an "overweight" position on plantations.

"Shares of the six plantation firms already trading on the market having appeciated over 100 percent since they were issued in 1995. This should act as a magnet," said Manjula de Silva, general manager of CTC Eagle Fund Management.
Sri Lanka, which began privatising management of its 23 plantation firms which own some 600,000 hectares of tea, rubber and coconut estates 1992, started selling ownership in 1995.
Six plantation firms are already listed on the CSE: Agalawatte Plantations, Kotagala Plantations, Kelani Valley Plantations, Kegalle Plantations, Bogawantalawa Plantations and Horana Plantations.
The average price of the six shares, which were all issued to the public at 10 rupees each, had risen to around 35 rupees by Monday.
Tea prices have been buoyed by strong demand from the countries of the former Soviet Union and the Middle East.
Most analysts believe the seven IPOs will be priced at discounts to current market prices.

"With the six listed shares trading at multiples of nine to 10 times earnings for the financial year to 31 March, 1998, the IPOs would probably be priced at about six to seven times," said Derendra Abayaratna, general manager of Equity Growth Fund.
De Silva of CTC Eagle Fund Management said the ideal price would be about 20 to 25 rupees a share.
PERC officials said they were keeping an open mind on price.
